name: Yawuru
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

new_statements.quote: Stress is not distinctive in Yawuru, at least in the sense that no pairs of words are distinguished on the basis of different stress positions with otherwise identical sequences of segmental phonemes. Stress in Yawuru, however, is not completely predictable, either. [§3.7.1.1 Primary stress] In the majority of words, primary stress (indicated by the acute accent mark) is assigned to the first syllable, regardless of the number of syllables or moras that make up the word. [fn. 130, p. 97:] A count based on a working vocabulary of 1730 nominals indicates that 1704 words (or over 98%) have their primary stress on the 1st syllable.
new_statements.citation: Hosokawa, Komei. 1991. The Yawuru language of West Kimberley: a meaning-based description. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. http://hdl.handle.net/1885/10851
new_statements.locator: p. 96, §3.7.1 Stress and §3.7.1.1 Primary stress (PDF page 128); count in fn. 130, p. 97 (PDF page 129); secondary stress p. 98, §3.7.1.2 (PDF page 130)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (556-page image scan, Canon iR7105, no text layer past the ANU cover sheet; 8,702,861 bytes). Rendered PDF pp. 128-129 (printed pp. 96-97) at 150 dpi and viewed them, plus a 300 dpi crop of fn. 130. The quoted passage is on the page word for word: p. 96 §3.7.1 "Stress is not distinctive in Yawuru, at least in the sense that no pairs of words are distinguished on the basis of different stress positions with otherwise identical sequences of segmental phonemes. Stress in Yawuru, however, is not completely predictable, either."; §3.7.1.1 "In the majority of words, primary stress (indicated by the acute accent mark) is assigned to the first syllable, regardless of the number of syllables…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word (over 98% of nominals), irrespective of word length or syllable weight. Stress is not contrastive, but it is lexically irregular in a small residue: a few dozen compounds, place names, onomatopoeic items and a handful of monomorphemic words carry primary stress on a later syllable, and interjections/onomatopoeics often show final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Described at length (pp. 98-102): words of more than three syllables usually carry a secondary stress placed by mora counting, where preconsonantal sonorant codas count as moras: "i) The 1st mora bears primary stress and the 3rd mora, if vocalic, bears secondary stress. ii) If the 3rd mora is a non-vocalic sonorant, then the vowel in the 4th mora takes up secondary stress, unless it is the word-final vowel." In reduplicated words secondary stress falls on the first vowel of the repeated half regardless of mora count (p. 102, §3.7.1.4); stress in conjugated verbs is treated separately (§3.7.1.5, not read here).
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 130: 2 words with primary stress on the 2nd syllable, 15 on the 3rd, 6 on the 4th, 8 on the 5th (mostly suspected compounds, toponyms, e.g. birdirlngaba, kabanyanya; a few monomorphemic words, e.g. dyararu 'spring country', bambida 'small dragon lizard'); interjections and onomatopoeics often word-final (kwala, wardaw); two bound forms with final stress (-nyarra, -aw). "Except for the onomatopoeic items... no phonological reason is found for the irregular stress distribution."
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from a dictionary count of 1730 nominals; verb roots, interjections and onomatopoeics excluded from the count; stress in conjugated verbs handled in a separate subsection.
new_statements.identity_note: Hosokawa describes Yawuru of the Broome area, West Kimberley, from work with the last fluent speakers in the 1980s; this is the language-level yawu1244 itself, no dialect split at issue. Glottolog 5.3 lists the language as extinct/reawakening.

sources.note: §3.7.1 (pp. 96-102): stress not distinctive but not fully predictable; primary stress on the first syllable in over 98% of nominals (1704/1730, fn. 130); the exceptions are compounds, toponyms, onomatopoeics and a handful of monomorphemic words; secondary stress is mora-counting (1st mora primary, 3rd mora secondary if vocalic, else the 4th-mora vowel unless word-final), with a separate pattern in reduplicated words (secondary on the first vowel of the repeated half) and a separate treatment of conjugated verbs (§3.7.1.5). Page images of pp. 96 and 98 checked by eye against the scanned.
